title: The Meta Settlement Proves the Child Safety Movement Was Right
gist: Meta settled with 47 state attorneys general who sued it for knowingly addicting children, agreeing to pay roughly $18 billion and to implement age-verification and other child-safety measures the tech-safety movement had pushed. IFS's Michael Toscano frames it as vindication but incomplete, noting the deal omits parental consent and does not bind other platforms.

insights.claim: Meta settled with 47 state attorneys general who jointly sued the company for knowingly addicting children to its platforms, agreeing to pay states approximately $18 billion.
insights.speaker: Michael Toscano
insights.so_what: A multi-billion-dollar regulatory settlement against a mega-cap platform signals rising legal/compliance liability across the social-media sector, not just for Meta.
insights.quote: While the financial amount that Meta agreed to pay the states may seem modest (approximately $18 billion), the details of the settlement are anything but
insights.locator: Those who were too far out of the range of the quake

insights.claim: Meta's settlement requires age-verification systems with a false-positive threshold of 3% for minors ages 13-15 and 10% for those ages 16-17, an accuracy standard the author contrasts favorably with Australia's social media law that mandates no accuracy threshold.
insights.speaker: Michael Toscano
insights.so_what: Concrete accuracy thresholds create a technical compliance benchmark that age-verification vendors and other platforms may be pushed to meet.
insights.quote: requiring them to use age verification systems with a false positive threshold of 3% for minors ages 13-15 and 10% for those ages 16-17
insights.locator: Fortunately, Meta's agreement solves that problem

insights.claim: The settlement commits Meta to measures including age verification to open a social media account plus default time limits, night mode, and school mode, but does not require parental consent for a child to access an account.
insights.speaker: Michael Toscano
insights.so_what: The omission of parental consent marks where future legislation and advocacy pressure will concentrate, shaping the next round of platform compliance requirements.
insights.quote: Nothing in Meta's settlement agreement requires that. This is a critical omission.
insights.locator: Despite how hard parents across the country have fought

insights.claim: IFS argues digital child safety must rest on age verification applied at two levels—the platform level and the app-store level—which it terms the 'double layer of protection,' with other remedies like time limits flowing through accurate age knowledge.
insights.speaker: Michael Toscano
insights.so_what: Framing age verification as a two-layer requirement implicates app-store owners (Apple, Google) as much as platforms, widening the regulatory perimeter for investors to watch.
insights.quote: age verification applied at two levels: the platform level and the app-store level

insights.claim: IFS co-authored the first policy paper calling for app-store-level age verification and continued advocating both platform- and app-store-level remedies even as companies like Meta treated the two approaches as competitive with each other.
insights.speaker: Michael Toscano
insights.so_what: The divergence between platforms and advocates over where verification sits signals a live policy fight that will determine which companies bear compliance costs.
insights.quote: While some groups and companies like Meta saw these ideas as competitive with each other, we continued to call for both remedies
insights.locator: In fact, IFS co-authored the first policy paper

insights.claim: In August 2022, IFS, the Ethics and Public Policy Center, and the Center for Renewing America released the policy brief 'Protecting Teens from Big Tech,' described as the first policy paper calling for age verification of social media.
insights.speaker: Michael Toscano
insights.so_what: Tracing the origin dates the policy trend, letting investors gauge how quickly advocacy ideas translate into binding platform obligations.
insights.quote: the very first policy paper calling for age verification of social media
insights.locator: In August 2022, the Institute for Family Studies

insights.claim: Less than a year after the 2022 IFS brief, Utah became the first state to require age verification for young Americans to open a social media account, and other states enacted similar laws that Big Tech trade associations then challenged in court.
insights.speaker: Michael Toscano
insights.so_what: State-by-state age-verification laws plus industry litigation create a patchwork of legal risk and compliance cost across social platforms.
insights.quote: this paper inspired a law in Utah, the first state in the country to require age verification for young Americans to open a social media account

insights.claim: The author calls for Congress to enact the Kids Online Safety Act, the App Store Accountability Act, the Guard Act, and the SCREEN Act, plus a bill codifying and strengthening Meta's settlement terms and extending them to all social media platforms.
insights.speaker: Michael Toscano
insights.so_what: These named bills are the forward pipeline of platform regulation; their progress is a concrete catalyst to monitor for sector-wide compliance exposure.
insights.quote: We need Congress to enact the Kids Online Safety Act, the App Store Accountability Act, the Guard Act, and the SCREEN Act
insights.locator: We need legislation that codifies this settlement

insights.claim: The author stresses that Meta is one of many offenders and that the same child-safety measures should be generalized across all social media platforms rather than confined to a single company's settlement.
insights.speaker: Michael Toscano
insights.so_what: Advocacy intent to universalize the terms signals that the compliance burden imposed on Meta is a template likely to spread to competitors.
insights.quote: we should not forget that many other social media platforms are also harming children. We need to apply these same measures to all social media platforms.
